newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Bank of Italy governor urges spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of Italy governor urges spending cuts.

text.p: Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said on Thursday it would be harder for him to bring down interest rates -- among the highest in Europe -- unless the government did more to cut spending.

In an unusually explicit statement to a parliamentary commission, Fazio said the government's recently unveiled three-year economic strategy, known as the DPEF, did not call for a big enough cut in expenditure.
Government spending targets contained in the DPEF, approved by the cabinet last month and currently being debated in parliament, were "excessive", Fazio told the commission.
"In the context of a structural overhaul in public finances, the fall in interest rates could be greater than forecast in the 1998-2000 DPEF," Fazio told the commission.
The government forecast that yields on 12-month bills (BOTs) would drop from an expected 6.5 percent at the end of 1997 to six percent in 1998, 5.7 percent in 1999 and 5.5 percent in 2000.

Lower interest rates bring big benefits to state finances by lowering the cost of servicing Italy's national debt mountain, which is equivalent to more than 120 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP).
He said the government should seek 10 trillion lire ($5.9 billion) of cuts from the welfare state in 1998 out of a total savings goal contained in the DPEF of 15 trillion lire.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition is due to start talks with union leaders later this month on a comprehensive reform of social spending.

The government has yet to state publicly the scale of welfare spending cuts it plans for next year but union officials said last month they had been told that up to seven trillion lire of cuts in pension benefits had been envisaged.
Fazio's insistence on the need for the government to maintain an onslaught on public spending signalled a shift of emphasis in the central bank governor's public statements.
"The governor is moving the emphasis to public spending whereas before there was more stress on inflation," said Francesco Giordano, an economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
Fazio said he would not lower interest rates immediately due to market turmoil but hoped for more room to do so in the future as the economy gradually gained strength.
"Not in the current time of turmoil but I hope to have in the future margins for a rate cut," he told a parliamentary budget commission.
He said he did not want to give the economy an artificial shot in the arm. "Don't ask me to force the economy or drug it."

Italy's gross domestic product slipped 0.5 percent year-on-year in the first quarter of the year, but Fazio said he expected average GDP in 1997 to grow between one and 1.2 percent. The government has forecast the economy will expand by 1.2 percent in the current year.

The central bank has been urged to cut its official discount rate in recent months, which has been held at 6.75 percent since mid-January, despite a sharp fall in inflation. Fazio is believed to be worried that inflation is falling primarily because of subdued demand.
Economists said there was room for a cut in borrowing costs.
"I think interest rates are excessive and if the central bank continues to disappoint market expectations it could cause confusion," said Riccardo Barbieri, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
